claims.text: Dynamic behavior in solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes is primarily governed by the interplay between dislocation mobility and lattice-level friction or incipient elastic instability.
The lattice-level friction or incipient elastic instability arises from intrinsic atomic-scale inhomogeneities.
The interplay between dislocation mobility and lattice-level friction enables FeNiCrMn to maintain a favorable strength-ductility balance under dynamic loading.
The proposed initial FeNiCrMn material has a homogeneous distribution of its constituent elements.
The proposed initial material is free from major secondary phases.
The proposed initial material is free from pre-existing large-scale defects.
Increasing strain rate reduces dislocation mobility through enhanced local lattice friction.
Lowering temperature reduces dislocation mobility through enhanced local lattice friction.
Local lattice friction is inherent to the alloy's atomic inhomogeneity.
Reduced dislocation mobility delays or modifies dislocation-slip events.
Delayed or modified slip events preserve the alloy's strength-ductility balance.
Lower strain rates or elevated temperatures enhance dislocation mobility and compensate for reduced lattice friction.
Yield strength, ductility, and strain-hardening behavior will shift systematically with temperature and strain rate.
Changes in yield strength, ductility, and strain hardening will correlate with measured changes in dislocation density, dislocation mobility, and indicators of local lattice friction.
Under quasi-static loading at room temperature, dislocation mechanisms dominate without significant contributions from variations in lattice friction.
At ultra-high strain rates, deep-cryogenic temperatures, or very high temperatures, mechanisms other than the proposed dislocation-friction interplay may dominate.
Trends from related high-entropy-alloy studies support a role for dislocation mobility and lattice friction.

Significant mechanical-property changes without measurable changes in dislocation mobility or lattice-distortion indicators would falsify the claim that the proposed interplay is the dominant mechanism.
